title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Customized prompt

I am creating a regression case study in R and Quarto. My question is: To what extent do incident type, institution size, and event year help predict reported economic losses from cyber incidents at financial institutions? The response is natural log of positive reported monetary loss in nominal USD. Predictors are incident type (physical or error, misuse or social, hacking or malware), institution size (up to 1,000 or over 1,000 employees), and incident year centered at 2013. The course-based core model is lm(log_loss ~ type + size + year_c). We have 26 incidents from 2002 to 2016. The baseline R-squared is 0.260. The estimated geometric mean loss ratio for larger versus smaller institutions is 12.0, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.28 to 521.5. Only five records involve smaller institutions, and none of those have misuse or social incidents. Suggest three feasible beyond-course extensions that strengthen this same regression question. For each, explain how it helps, how its result would enter the case study, the implementation steps, and two independent checks. Keep repeated cross-validation and influence sensitivity as the two separate course-method elements. Do not choose for me.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Proposed extension
We selected an interactive display of the regression predictions and their 95% confidence intervals. Readers will choose incident type, institution size, and a year from 2002 to 2016. The display will show how predictions and uncertainty change and flag groups with no observations. We will include it in the case-study page with a short explanation of what it adds to our research question.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Two planned verification checks

Compare with R: Compare the display’s predictions and interval endpoints with saved results from predict.lm for both size groups and all incident types. Check the controls and warnings. Use the official R documentation to confirm the meaning of the confidence intervals.
Manual calculation: For one supported example, calculate the prediction from the model coefficients. Calculate the confidence interval using the coefficient covariance matrix and the t critical value with 21 residual degrees of freedom. Compare it with R and the display.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Decisions and limitation
We chose the interactive display because it helps explain the wide uncertainty in our baseline. We did not select a random forest because our sample is small. We will label exponentiated predictions as geometric mean losses. The display cannot fix missing loss data or the small sample.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Data source
We use the VERIS Community Database (VCDB). Each row is one incident. The response is reported loss in USD. Predictors are incident type, employee-count category, and incident year.
The code below embeds 61 finance-and-insurance records with positive reported losses. Keeping USD records with known size and year, and excluding a security-budget amount and an unrelated fine, leaves 26 incidents. Public reports are not a random sample, and missing losses are not zero.
The embedded data are adapted from VCDB under CC BY-SA 4.0. No customer or employee identifiers are included. The code contains the data and preparation steps needed to reproduce the baseline.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Baseline
Our baseline predicts natural log loss from incident type, institution size, and year. Its R-squared is 0.260. The estimated loss ratio for larger versus smaller institutions is 12.0, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.28 to 521.5. Only five incidents involve smaller institutions, so the comparison is uncertain.
